sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Existing salvage therapies for recurrent glioblastoma (rGBM) have limited efficacy, with a median survival of approximately 9 months. Given the complex molecular heterogeneity of GBM, single-target approaches have consistently failed as a treatment strategy. We conducted a phase I clinical trial to assess the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of a genomically tailored multiagent regimen in 30 adults with surgically treated rGBM.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: Adults with IDH wild-type GBM (n = 29) or grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytoma (n = 1) were consented and underwent clinically indicated surgery for recurrent disease. Comprehensive genomic profiling was performed on the recurrent tumors, and results for each patient were discussed at an individualized molecular tumor board to determine a personalized treatment regimen combining up to four FDA-approved drugs, including one cytotoxic agent as the backbone.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: A total of 12 drugs were used in 18 combinations—the most common regimen was lomustine, afatinib, and abemaciclib (n = 8). The most common toxicities included cytopenias, rash, and gastrointestinal symptoms, requiring frequent dose reductions. Measured from surgery at trial enrollment, progression-free survival at 6 months was 40%, overall survival (OS) at 9 months was 73%, and median OS was 12.7 months. After trial therapy, genomic profiling performed on subsequent recurrent tumor specimens identified genetic evolution corresponding to putative treatment resistance mechanisms.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Implementation of individualized treatment regimens in a timely fashion was feasible for patients with surgically resectable rGBM. Overall efficacy was not significantly improved compared with a contemporary patient cohort treated without experimental regimens, with full dosing of most combination therapies limited by toxicities.

boxed-text.p: Despite decades of clinical trials testing new experimental therapies, new effective single agents that extend survival for patients with glioblastoma (GBM) have not been identified. One potential approach that has not been extensively tested to date is the combination of multiple targeted therapy drugs in a genomically tailored precision medicine regimen. We conducted a first-in-class phase I clinical trial administering up to three FDA-approved targeted agents in addition to a cytotoxic backbone agent in adults with recurrent GBM (rGBM). This study confirmed the feasibility of a genomically tailored treatment approach in the rGBM setting, revealed that full dosing of multiagent combination therapies was often limited by toxicities, and demonstrated modest efficacy when compared with a matched cohort of patients with surgically treated rGBM who received only salvage cytotoxic chemotherapy ± additional radiotherapy without experimental agents.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: IDH wild-type glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults, with approximately 13,000 patients diagnosed each year in the United States (1). Approximately half of patients with GBM die within the first 15 months of diagnosis, and nearly all succumb to the disease within 5 years (2). The standard of care for newly diagnosed GBM consists of maximal safe surgical resection to remove or debulk the tumor mass, followed by external beam radiotherapy and 6 to 12 cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy with the alkylating agent temozolomide (TMZ), with or without “tumor treating fields” (3). Despite this aggressive treatment, GBM invariably recurs, with a median time to progression of less than 12 months. Average survival from this time of recurrent disease is approximately 9 months (2). There is no standardized therapy established for recurrent/progressive GBM (rGBM). Many treatments are commonly employed, including bevacizumab, nitrosoureas, re-resection, reirradiation, or enrollment in a clinical trial (2). However, no class of agents has yet proven to yield a survival advantage at the time of GBM recurrence. Furthermore, clinical trial design and evaluation of anticancer therapeutics in the rGBM population are hampered by several crucial issues: intratumoral genetic heterogeneity, interpatient tumor heterogeneity, the genetic evolution of tumors at recurrence, and a limited understanding of tumoral resistance mechanisms to standard treatment (4–8). To address the dismal prognosis of patients with rGBM, it is essential to transform traditional clinical trial paradigms to allow for rapid and efficient therapy development (9).

Somatic alterations, including point mutations, short insertion/deletion mutations, focal gene amplifications and deletions, chromosomal gains and losses, and chromosomal rearrangements, including translocations and other structural variants, are well known to occur at the DNA level in human cancers. These somatic genetic events activate oncogenes and inactivate tumor suppressor genes that fuel tumor initiation, malignant progression, metastatic spread, and drug resistance (10). Advances in next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have provided the ability to efficiently and rapidly interrogate each patient’s tumor for the complete spectrum of genetic aberrations known to drive oncogenesis at an affordable cost. This enables the incorporation of molecular profiling of individual tumor specimens into real-time disease classification and treatment decision-making (11). As such, we are now able to accurately classify each patient’s tumor using the combination of traditional histopathology and NGS profiling, assess whether a tumor is sporadic due to exclusively somatic genetic alterations or syndromic due to an underlying constitutional/germline variant, and identify any potentially targetable oncogenic alterations associated with sensitivity to targeted small-molecule inhibitors or monoclonal antibodies (12, 13). As our understanding of the prognostic importance of specific molecular features has increased, this has led to the recategorization of central nervous system (CNS) tumors into more homogeneous tumor types. For example, tumors that were categorized as IDH-mutant GBM in the 2016 World Health Organization (WHO) Classification were recategorized in the 2021 WHO Classification as grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytomas, in recognition of their different underlying biology and more favorable prognosis (2).

Given this advancement, there has been an explosion of interest in applying new targeted anticancer agents to treat GBM that might be more efficacious with fewer adverse side effects than standard cytotoxic chemotherapy. Such molecularly targeted therapies have shown success in other solid tumor types, including trastuzumab targeting breast cancers with HER2/ERBB2 amplification, erlotinib targeting lung cancers with EGFR kinase domain mutations, imatinib targeting gastrointestinal stromal tumors with KIT mutations, vemurafenib targeting melanomas with the BRAF p.V600E mutation, and others (14). In contrast, clinical trials with dozens of such targeted agents in patients with GBM over the past two decades have all failed to produce a significant survival benefit (15). However, these agents have mainly been tested in genetically unselected patient cohorts and frequently tested as single agents. We now appreciate that GBM is a genetically complex disease, with most tumors harboring at least four or five different oncogenic aberrations affecting multiple intracellular pathways, including telomere maintenance, cell-cycle regulation, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, Ras-MAP kinase signaling, PI3-kinase-Akt-mTOR signaling, p53/apoptosis regulation, and chromatin modification/remodeling (16). As such, most investigators envision that utilizing multiple agents simultaneously to target various alterations in a patient’s GBM is more likely to be efficacious than single-agent therapy, but identifying which combination of agents to use to target a patient’s specific molecular composition and implementing such treatment in a timely fashion has been challenging to date. In particular, FDA-approved oncologic drugs, both targeted and traditional cytotoxic agents, are expensive, and the vast majority are not approved for GBM. Obtaining third-party payor approval to use these drugs for patients in an off-label fashion is arduous, time-consuming, and frequently unsuccessful, even for a single drug, let alone for multiple drugs in a bespoke fashion.

In a prior pilot study, we demonstrated the feasibility of obtaining genomic data for adult patients with surgically resected rGBM and using it to generate patient-specific therapeutic drug regimens based on expert analysis of the molecular profile that incorporated consideration of potential drug–drug interactions, overlapping drug toxicities, and penetration of the drug into the CNS (17). However, the choice of whether to implement the recommended regimen was left to the patient and the treating physician, and obtaining third-party payor approval for such off-label use was frequently challenging and slow. Here, we report the design, performance, and results of a phase I clinical trial evaluating not only the feasibility of generating a patient-specific drug regimen recommendation in patients with surgically resectable rGBM but also initiating treatment within a clinically relevant time frame after surgery and determining the efficacy of this multiagent precision medicine approach. Notably, funding for this trial included coverage of the cost of the oncologic agents, eliminating the need for third-party payor approvals and enabling the successful initiation of a precision medicine treatment regimen in all 30 patients who underwent surgery with pathologically confirmed rGBM.

sec.title: Trial design and patient population
sec.p: We performed a single-arm, nonrandomized open-label phase I clinical trial assessing the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of genomically tailored individualized multiagent treatment regimens in 30 patients with surgically resected rGBM (ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT03681028). The initial cohort enrolled 15 patients with the primary objective of evaluating the feasibility of initiating an individualized treatment regimen in a timely fashion, defined as within 35 days of surgery. Secondary objectives included the safety of the individualized regimen, as well as efficacy measured by progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). Subsequently, an expansion cohort of 15 patients was added to improve power for the preliminary assessment of efficacy. All patients signed informed consent and were registered for the study prior to a scheduled, clinically indicated surgery. After pathologic confirmation of rGBM (either IDH wild-type GBM or IDH-mutant astrocytoma, CNS WHO grade 4), genomic profiling was performed on the collected tumor specimen. A multidisciplinary tumor board then reviewed the genomic sequencing results in the context of the patient’s history and prior therapy to generate an individualized treatment recommendation. The recommended treatment, combining up to four FDA-approved drugs, including one cytotoxic agent as a backbone, was to be initiated within 35 days after surgery. Patients were monitored for any treatment-associated toxicities throughout the duration of the trial via physical exams and serologic studies assessing blood counts, kidney function, liver function, and other values as clinically indicated based on selected therapies. Dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) was defined as follows: (i) any grade 3 or 4 nonhematologic toxicity attributable to study therapy [excluding alopecia, nausea/vomiting/diarrhea, or rash not maximally treated with supportive therapy; laboratory abnormalities (e.g., cholesterol or phosphorus) unless persistent despite maximal treatment; seizures; and thrombotic disease (unless a known risk for the study agent)] or (ii) any grade 4 neutropenia or thrombocytopenia. The initial cohort included a safety stopping rule with a pause in enrollment and review by the Data Safety Monitoring Committee to determine next steps if ≥3 of the 15 patients experienced DLTs, and the same rule was used as a guide in the expansion cohort. Imaging for response assessment was performed every 8 weeks using MR imaging. Treatment continued until tumor progression. The UCSF Institutional Review Board approved the trial protocol (IRB# 18-24939), which was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Exclusion and inclusion criteria
sec.p: Patients >18 years old with recurrent, surgically resectable GBM or gliosarcoma (by the 2016 WHO Classification of CNS Tumors guidelines for the initial cohort and by the 2021 WHO Classification guidelines for the expansion cohort) were potential candidates. An expectation for at least 500 mg of resectable tumor tissue was required. Other eligibility criteria included a Karnofsky performance status score of ≥70, an estimated life expectancy of ≥3 months, appropriate prior therapy at the time of initial diagnosis (any number of recurrences was allowed), and adequate bone marrow function, renal function, and hepatic function. Adequate bone marrow function was defined by an absolute neutrophil count of ≥1,500/μL and platelets of ≥100,000/μL; adequate hepatic function was determined by total bilirubin of ≤1.5× the institutional upper limit of normal, aspartate aminotransferase of ≤2.5× the institutional upper limit of normal, and alanine aminotransferase of ≤2.5× the institutional upper limit of normal; adequate renal function was defined by serum creatinine of ≤1.5× the institutional upper limit of normal or creatinine clearance of ≥60 mL/minutes/1.73 m2. Exclusion criteria included the presence of New York Heart Association grade II or greater congestive heart failure, a history of myocardial infarction or unstable angina within 12 months prior to study enrollment, receipt of cancer treatment within 4 weeks prior to study registration, failure to recover from the adverse effects of previous treatment, the presence of another active malignancy, known human immunodeficiency virus–positive status, or other concurrent medical conditions that were felt to elevate the risk associated with trial therapy. Patients whose resected tissue revealed predominantly treatment effects rather than viable tumors such that genomic profiling could not be successfully completed, were excluded as screen failures. In addition, patients who had a treatment plan successfully generated but who were unable to start treatment due to an extenuating circumstance, like postoperative infection, were also excluded as screen failures. All patients receiving at least one dose of any of the precision medicine trial regimen drugs were included in the as-treated population for the efficacy endpoints.

sec.title: IHC and MGMT promoter methylation testing
sec.p: IHC was performed using the following antibodies as previously described: phosphorylated p44/42 ERK1/2 Thr202/Tyr204 (Cell Signaling Technology, RRID:AB_2315112, clone D13.14.4E, cat. #4370, 1:10,000 dilution) and phosphorylated S6 ribosomal protein Ser240/244 (Cell Signaling Technology, RRID:AB_331682, polyclonal cat. #2215, 1:50 dilution; refs. 18–20). DNA methylation at 17 CpG sites in the MGMT promoter region was assessed by targeted bisulfite sequencing in a Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA)–certified clinical laboratory as previously described, with tumors having methylation at 0 to 2 sites classified as hypo/unmethylated and those having methylation at 3 to 17 sites classified as hypermethylated (21).

sec.title: Tumor genomic profiling
sec.p: Genomic DNA was extracted from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue of the rGBM tumor specimens from the 30 patients using the QIAamp DNA FFPE Tissue Kit (QIAGEN). Tumor tissue was selectively scraped from unstained slides or punched from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded blocks using biopsy punches (Integra Miltex Instruments) to enrich for maximal tumor content (ideally >25% tumor fraction). For most patients (n = 27, as indicated), a constitutional DNA sample was extracted from a buccal swab or peripheral blood specimen using the QIAamp DNA Blood Midi Kit (QIAGEN) and simultaneously sequenced to enable accurate discrimination of germline versus somatic origin of variants. Capture-based next-generation DNA sequencing was performed on a clinical basis in a CLIA-certified laboratory using the UCSF500 NGS panel, as previously described, that targets all coding exons of 529 cancer-related genes, select introns and upstream regulatory regions of 73 genes to enable detection of structural variants, including gene fusions, and DNA segments at regular intervals along each chromosome to enable genome-wide copy-number and zygosity analysis, with a total sequencing footprint of 2.8 Mb (12, 22–25). This assay typically provides greater than 500× mean on-target sequencing coverage over the IDH1 p.R132 and IDH2 p.R172 mutational hotspots, as well as a comprehensive assessment of cytogenetic alterations (e.g., chromosomes 1p and 19q status, chromosomes 7 and 10 status) and genetic alterations (e.g., EGFR, PDGFRA, MET, FGFR3, NTRK1-3, PTPN11, NF1, BRAF, PIK3CA, PIK3R1, PTEN, CDKN2A, CDKN2C, CDK4, CDK6, RB1, TP53, MDM2, MDM4, H3F3A, HIST1H3B, CIC, FUBP1, NOTCH1, TCF12, STAG2, ATRX, TERT promoter) critical for glioma diagnostic assessment. Multiplex library preparation was performed using the KAPA HyperPrep Kit (Roche) according to the manufacturer’s specifications with 200 ng of sample DNA. Hybrid capture of pooled libraries was performed using a custom oligonucleotide library (Integrated DNA Technologies). Captured libraries were sequenced as paired-end reads on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 instrument. Sequence reads were mapped to the reference human genome build GRCh37 (hg19) using the Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (RRID:SCR_010910). Recalibration and deduplication of reads were performed using the Genome Analysis Toolkit (RRID:SCR_001876). Coverage and sequencing statistics were determined using Picard CalculateHsMetrics and Picard CollectInsertSizeMetrics (RRID:SCR_006525). Single-nucleotide variant and insertion/deletion mutation calling was performed with FreeBayes (RRID:SCR_010761), UnifiedGenotyper, and Pindel (RRID:SCR_000560). Structural rearrangement calling was performed with Delly (RRID:SCR_004603). Single-nucleotide variants, insertions/deletions, and structural variants were visualized and verified using Integrative Genome Viewer. Genome-wide copy-number and zygosity analysis was performed by CNVkit (26) and visualized using Nexus Copy Number (Biodiscovery, RRID:SCR_004557). Microsatellite instability determination was performed with MSIsensor2 analysis of mono- and dinucleotide repeats (27). GBMs were deemed positive for microsatellite instability when ≥10% of the 86 microsatellites assessed by the UCSF500 NGS panel were unstable. Somatic tumor mutational burden (TMB) was determined by calculating the number of somatic mutations in the coding regions of genes in the UCSF500 NGS panel, counting both single-nucleotide variants and short indels, divided by the total coding footprint of the assay (1.5 Mb). For patients with paired tumor–normal sequencing performed, TMB was calculated using only the confirmed somatic mutations. For patients with tumor-only sequencing performed, TMB was calculated by removing known germline variants present at ≥0.001% frequency in human population datasets (ExAC, gnomAD, and NHLBI-ESP6515). Hypermutation was defined as those tumors with TMB values of ≥15 somatic mutations per Mb based on this assay. TMZ-induced hypermutation was defined as those rGBMs demonstrating somatic hypermutation acquired specifically at the time of recurrence following adjuvant chemotherapy that was not present in the matched initial treatment-naïve tumor and was characterized by a mutational signature with a predominance of C>T:G>A transitions (28–30). Each of the confirmed somatic variants from paired tumor–normal sequencing or filtered variants from tumor-only sequencing analysis was reviewed for predicted oncogenicity/pathogenicity using known cancer genomics data in the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (http://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic; RRID:SCR_002260) and cBioPortal (http://www.cbioportal.org/) databases, location within the encoded protein, and predicted functional effect based on mutation type (e.g., missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice site).

sec.title: Genomically tailored treatment selection
sec.p: A multidisciplinary tumor board was convened for each patient at the completion of genomic profiling to determine a recommended precision medicine treatment regimen that combined up to four FDA-approved drugs, including one cytotoxic agent as the backbone. This tumor board consisted of the study principal investigator (J.L. Clarke), the study neuropathologist and genomics investigator (D.A. Solomon), a clinical pharmacist with expertise in oncologic therapeutics (J.A. Grabowsky), a pharmacologist with expertise in pharmacogenetics (D.L. Kroetz), neuro-oncologists including the patient’s treating physician (N.A. Oberheim Bush, C. Kline, J.W. Taylor, J.F. de Groot, N.A. Butowski, S.M. Chang, and J.L. Clarke), and other neuro-oncology team members including the clinical research coordinator (M. Tedesco) and nurse manager (J. Rabbitt). Considerations when deciding upon the specific multiagent drug regimen included (i) the genetic alterations identified in the tumor either known or predicted to be associated with sensitivity to specific targeted inhibitors, (ii) blood-brain barrier penetration of the agents being considered, (iii) MGMT promoter methylation status, (iv) prior responsiveness and tolerance to adjuvant TMZ and other therapies used prior to trial enrollment, (v) known or predicted drug–drug interactions and toxicity profiles, and (vi) patient functional status and predicted tolerance of anticipated toxicities. The selection and prioritization of agents recommended by the tumor board followed a tiered ranking system modeled after the European Society for Molecular Oncology Scale for Clinical Actionability of Molecular Targets (31). The cytotoxic backbone agent was TMZ, lomustine (CCNU), or carboplatin. TMZ was used for patients with MGMT promoter–methylated GBM, unless they had previously progressed while on TMZ or their tumor had developed treatment-induced hypermutation. CCNU was used for patients with MGMT promoter–unmethylated GBM or those whose tumors had developed treatment-induced hypermutation. For those patients who had previously progressed on CCNU, carboplatin was used. The PARP inhibitor olaparib was recommended in combination with TMZ based on expected synergy in MGMT promoter–methylated GBMs (32, 33). The cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) 4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib was recommended in the context of those GBMs with intact/wild-type RB1 alleles harboring CDKN2A homozygous deletion or CDK4 amplification, based on multiple preclinical studies providing evidence for this strategy (34–36). The second-generation EGFR inhibitor afatinib was recommended in the context of those GBMs harboring EGFR alterations, including amplification, intragenic deletion, and activating missense mutations, based on its known blood-brain barrier penetration and prior clinical trial safety data in patients with rGBM (37). Other targeted agents that were recommended included the MEK inhibitor trametinib (usually in the context of inactivating NF1 mutations/deletions), the multikinase inhibitor dasatinib (in the context of PDGFRA amplification), the FGFR family kinase inhibitor erdafitinib (in the context of FGFR3::TACC3 fusion), the PI3-kinase inhibitor alpelisib (in the context of PIK3CA activating mutation), and the mTOR inhibitor everolimus (usually in the context of PIK3CA, PIK3R1, or PTEN mutations or deletions).

sec.title: Endpoint assessment
sec.p: The primary endpoint of the initial cohort was the feasibility of starting treatment with the individualized treatment regimen within 35 days of surgery, with success defined as a target of 85% or greater. The primary endpoint for the combined cohort was the 9-month OS (OS-9) rate, with a null hypothesis of 50% and an alternative hypothesis of 75% (2), with an alpha of 2.5% and the null being rejected if ≥21 patients survived past 9 months from the trial enrollment surgery. Rejection of the null hypothesis would mean that it is very unlikely (<2.5% chance) that the true OS-9 of this trial cohort and treatment approach is equivalent to that of historical controls (OS-9 of 50%); however, this would not necessarily mean that the alternative hypothesis of OS-9 of ≥75% has been confirmed. Secondary endpoints for both the initial cohort and the combined cohort included safety, 6-month PFS (PFS-6), median PFS (mPFS), and median OS (mOS). Safety and severity of the adverse event profile were graded by the NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0 from the initiation of study therapy through the 30-day safety monitoring time frame after the last administration of the study regimen.

sec.title: Comparator cohort for assessment of trial efficacy
sec.p: Clinical outcomes for the 30 trial patients were assessed relative to a comparator cohort of 43 adult patients with IDH wild-type GBM treated with standard external beam radiation and adjuvant TMZ, who had undergone surgical resection at first recurrence followed by salvage radiation and/or cytotoxic chemotherapy (TMZ, CCNU, or carboplatin) without the use of targeted therapy agents or other experimental approaches. This comparator cohort was composed of adult patients at initial diagnosis who underwent two or more longitudinal surgical resections at UCSF Medical Center between 2003 and 2022, with pathologically confirmed IDH wild-type and histone H3 wild-type GBM located in the cerebral hemispheres (38).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using R (version 4.4.1, The R Project for Statistical Computing, RRID:SCR_001905). Categorical variables are presented as counts and frequencies, whereas continuous data are presented as median, mean (± SD), and range as indicated. Kaplan–Meier plots were used to estimate PFS and OS from trial enrollment surgery until disease recurrence or death. Median estimated survival with 95% confidence intervals and exact P values were calculated using the log-rank test. The proportion of patients achieving PFS-6 and OS-9 from trial enrollment surgery was also calculated. Fisher’s exact test was used to compare differences in PFS-6 and OS-9 proportions between the trial cohort and the comparator cohort.

sec.title: Genomic alteration evolution
sec.p: For a subset of patients (n = 9), a subsequent surgical resection was performed upon disease progression during the precision medicine clinical trial regimen. Genomic profiling using the identical platform and methodology was performed on these post–clinical trial treatment tumor specimens, enabling the study of the evolution of genetic alterations that occurred in response to the multiagent targeted therapy regimen. Those patients with an identical set of oncogenic genetic alterations between the two longitudinal tumor specimens, without private oncogenic variants in either tumor, were classified as “stable.” Those patients with genetic alterations private to the recurrent tumor specimen at the time of clinical trial enrollment that were absent in the subsequent specimen after the treatment regimen, or vice versa, were classified as “divergent.”

sec.title: Characteristics of rGBM clinical trial patient cohort
sec.p: The initial cohort was enrolled and underwent trial surgery between December 2018 and January 2020, and the expansion cohort was enrolled and underwent trial surgery between October 2021 and January 2023 (Table 1; Supplementary Tables S1 and S2). For the 30 patients in the combined trial cohort, there were 18 males and 12 females, with a median age at the time of initial diagnosis of 53 years (range 30–69). All tumors were located supratentorially, with 29 centered in the cerebral hemispheres and 1 centered in the thalamus. Twenty-nine patients had an integrated diagnosis of GBM, whereas one (patient 10) had an integrated diagnosis of IDH-mutant astrocytoma that was CNS WHO grade 4 at the time of trial enrollment surgery. Among the 30 patients, all had been treated with adjuvant radiation after their initial surgery, and 29 had been treated with adjuvant TMZ after their initial surgery (patient 15 received adjuvant nivolumab on a clinical trial instead of TMZ). At the time of trial enrollment surgery, 23 patients were experiencing their first recurrence, whereas 6 were at second recurrence (patients 15, 24, 25, 30, 31, and 41), and 1 was at third recurrence (patient 6). The tumor at trial enrollment surgery was a local disease recurrence at the prior resection cavity site in 28 patients, whereas it was distant from the prior resection cavity and mostly outside the prior radiation treatment field in 2 patients (patients 4 and 27). The baseline patient characteristics at the time of trial enrollment were comparable for the initial and expansion cohorts.

sec.title: Genomic profiling results for rGBM trial cohort
sec.p: Comprehensive genomic profiling was performed on the rGBM tumor specimens for the 30 trial patients, interrogating mutations, focal amplifications, deletions, gene fusions, and other structural variants in all known glioma oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (Fig. 1; Supplementary Tables S3–S5). The most frequent genetic alterations included TERT promoter hotspot mutation (25/30, 83%), CDKN2A homozygous/biallelic deletion (25/30, 83%), EGFR focal amplification often with accompanying intragenic deletion or missense mutation on the amplified alleles (17/30, 57%), PTEN inactivating mutation or homozygous deletion (15/30, 50%), TP53 inactivating mutation (8/30, 27%), NF1 inactivating mutation or homozygous deletion (7/30, 23%), MDM2 or MDM4 focal amplification (7/30, 23%), PIK3CA or PIK3R1 mutation (5/30, 17%), and CDK4 focal amplification (4/30, 13%). Other less common oncogenic events included PDGFRA amplification (3%), PTPRZ1::MET fusion (3%), FGFR3::TACC3 fusion (3%), PTPN11 mutation (10%), BRAF mutation (3%), RB1 mutation/deletion (3%), and CDKN2C homozygous deletion (7%). One tumor (patient 37) had acquired somatic hypermutation due to TMZ alkylating chemotherapy, whereas the other 29 patients’ tumors all had a low somatic mutation burden (<10 mutations per Mb). These genomic results align with the observed frequencies described in other cohorts of patients with GBM including specifically recurrent disease (16, 38).

sec.title: Genomically tailored multiagent treatment regimen
sec.p: A multidisciplinary tumor board was convened for each patient at the completion of genomic profiling to determine a recommended precision medicine treatment regimen that combined up to four FDA-approved drugs, including one cytotoxic agent as the backbone (Fig. 1; Supplementary Table S1; example tumor board report shown in Supplementary Item S1). A total of 12 different FDA-approved drugs were recommended in 18 different combinations for the 30-patient trial cohort, reflective of the substantial genetic and clinical heterogeneity of GBM.

sec.title: Feasibility of precision medicine treatment initiation
sec.p: All 15 of the patients in the initial cohort successfully started treatment within 35 days of their surgery, confirming that this approach was feasible to implement. Although it was not a study endpoint for the expansion cohort, 14 out of 15 of those patients also successfully started treatment within 35 days of their surgery. The median time to treatment initiation was 34 days from the trial enrollment surgery in both the initial (range 29–35 days) and expansion cohorts (range 27–36 days).

sec.title: Patient safety and toxicities experienced during the trial
sec.p: As anticipated, the trial patients experienced a range of treatment-related toxicities related to the multiagent precision medicine therapeutic regimens (Fig. 2; Supplementary Table S6). The first two patients treated in the initial cohort (patients 2 and 3) both received the combination of CCNU (90 mg/m2 every 8 weeks) + afatinib 40 mg daily (starting cycle 1, day 7) + abemaciclib 150 mg BID (starting cycle 1, day 29). Both patients required dose reductions of afatinib and abemaciclib due to grade 3 neutropenia with grade 2 diarrhea for patient 2 and grade 3 diarrhea with grade 3 dehydration for patient 3. As such, afatinib and abemaciclib were each started at one dose level reduction (30 mg daily and 100 mg BID, respectively) for all future patients in the trial. There were two DLTs during the clinical trial: diarrhea and resulting dehydration in patient 3 and grade 4 thrombocytopenia in patient 9. In addition, although not meeting formal DLT criteria, several treatment regimens resulted in overlapping toxicities, such that dose reduction or discontinuation of one or more drugs was needed for tolerability in 15 additional patients. In total, 18 of the 30 trial patients (60%) had to dose reduce, discontinue, or not initiate one or more of the recommended drugs composing the prescribed clinical trial regimen. Among the eight patients receiving the most common treatment regimen of CCNU + afatinib + abemaciclib, the most common grade 2 or 3 adverse events were neutropenia (n = 7 patients), fatigue (n = 4), diarrhea (n = 3), and rash (n = 3). Among the four patients receiving the second most common treatment regimen of TMZ + olaparib + afatinib, the most common grade 2 or 3 adverse events were neutropenia (n = 4 patients), rash (n = 2), and mucositis (n = 2).

sec.title: Efficacy of the clinical trial treatment regimens
sec.p: A swimmer plot of the 30-patient trial cohort showing the timing of initial surgical intervention, adjuvant radiation and chemotherapy, clinical trial enrollment at the time of surgical resection of rGBM, duration of the precision medicine clinical trial treatment regimen, and subsequent disease progression and death is shown in Fig. 3 (source data in Supplementary Table S1). PFS-6 for the initial cohort was 40%, with 6 of 15 patients remaining recurrence-free at 6 months following trial enrollment surgery. This PFS-6 rate was felt to be promising enough to add an expansion cohort of 15 additional patients to improve the power of efficacy assessment. The protocol was thus amended to enroll an expansion cohort of 15 additional patients, with the primary endpoint for the combined 30-patient cohort of OS-9 following trial enrollment surgery. For the combined 30-patient cohort, PFS-6 was 40%, with mPFS of 4.7 months [Fig. 4A, 95% confidence interval (CI), 3.1–6.7 months], OS-9 of 73%, and mOS of 12.7 months (Fig. 4B, 95% CI, 10.9–17.9 months). For just the 29 patients with IDH wild-type GBM, PFS-6 was 38%, with mPFS of 4.6 months, OS-9 of 72%, and mOS of 12.6 months.

sec.p: Clinical outcomes for the combined clinical trial cohort were assessed relative to a comparator cohort of 43 adult patients with supratentorial IDH wild-type GBM treated with standard external beam radiation and adjuvant TMZ who had undergone surgical resection at first recurrence followed by cytotoxic chemotherapy (TMZ, CCNU, or carboplatin) with or without salvage reirradiation but without the use of any targeted therapy agents or other experimental approaches (Supplementary Tables S7–S9; ref. 38). The mOS of this comparator cohort from the time of first surgically treated recurrence was 9.1 months (Fig. 4C, 95% CI, 8.2–12.1 months), with OS-9 of 51%. However, these differences between the mOS and OS-9 in this comparator cohort versus the trial cohort were not statistically significant (log-rank test P value = 0.52 and Fisher’s exact test P value = 0.14, respectively). When comparing survival with the comparator cohort, the one patient with IDH-mutant astrocytoma from the trial cohort was excluded from the analyses (Fig. 4C–F). To enhance the similarity of the two patient cohorts being compared in this survival analysis, we performed additional analyses that limited the trial cohort to only those 22 patients with IDH wild-type GBM who were enrolled at first recurrence and who had an mOS from trial enrollment surgery of 12.5 months (Fig. 4D and F, 95% CI, 10.4–17.9 months). We also limited the comparator cohort to those 34 patients who received salvage cytotoxic chemotherapy alone without additional salvage reirradiation and who had an mOS from the first surgically treated recurrence of 8.8 months (Fig. 4E and F, 95% CI, 7.8–11.8 months). Although there was improved survival length in the clinical trial cohort relative to the comparator cohort in each of the different comparisons, no statistically significant differences were found in any of the comparisons.

sec.title: Longitudinal genomic profiling reveals potential therapeutic resistance mechanisms
sec.p: For a subset of the trial patients (n = 9), a subsequent surgical resection was performed upon disease progression after the precision medicine clinical trial regimen. Genomic profiling using the identical platform and methodology was performed on these post–clinical trial tumor specimens, enabling the study of the evolution of genetic alterations that occurred in response to the multiagent targeted therapy regimen (Fig. 5; Supplementary Table S10). Five patients had stable genomes at recurrence posttrial therapy with identical oncogenic alterations and without an identifiable genetic evolution mechanism (Fig. 5A). One patient (25), whose rGBM at trial enrollment harbored both the BRAF p.D594N missense mutation and two deleterious NF1 mutations, developed newly acquired PIK3CA missense mutation and PTEN frameshift mutation, arising from a subclone without the BRAF mutation at recurrence after having received trial therapy with TMZ, olaparib, and the small-molecule MEK inhibitor trametinib (Fig. 5B). IHC staining for phospho-ERK1/2 and phospho-S6 proteins on both the trial enrollment surgery and posttrial therapy resection specimens revealed a decrease in phospho-ERK1/2 abundance and a robust increase in phospho-S6 abundance. These findings suggest that a shift from the RAS-MAPK pathway to the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway activation may have driven resistance to trametinib in this patient. Two patients (7 and 13) with IDH wild-type GBM, whose precision medicine regimen included TMZ as the cytotoxic backbone agent together with the PARP inhibitor olaparib, developed new inactivating mutations in a DNA mismatch repair gene (MSH6 or MSH2) and TMZ-induced hypermutation including new EGFR, TP53, and other oncogenic mutations at recurrence posttrial therapy (Fig. 5C). One patient (19) with IDH wild-type GBM, whose precision medicine regimen included TMZ as the cytotoxic backbone agent together with olaparib, developed newly acquired focal high-level amplification of the MGMT gene on chromosome 10q26.3 at recurrence posttrial therapy (Fig. 5D). Together, these longitudinal genomic profiling results after targeted therapy regimens reveal that diverse acquired therapeutic resistance mechanisms may underlie GBM progression.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We enrolled and treated 30 patients with surgically resectable rGBM in a precision medicine clinical trial employing a genomically tailored multiagent drug regimen based on the results of targeted next-generation DNA sequencing performed on the recurrent tumor specimens. The trial demonstrated feasibility and safety and met the primary efficacy endpoint of an OS-9 fraction of 73% that was greater than that of historical controls (i.e., null hypothesis of 50%). However, the combination regimens were difficult to tolerate, leading to frequent dose reductions and discontinuation of one or more agents, and the median survival from the time of trial enrollment surgery was only modestly longer and not significantly different from a contemporary comparator cohort.

Longitudinal genomic profiling of recurrent tumor specimens after the precision medicine trial regimen revealed potential therapeutic resistance mechanisms. One patient whose regimen included TMZ developed newly acquired focal MGMT gene amplification that likely drove resistance via increased repair of alkylated DNA within tumor cells. Other patients whose regimens included both TMZ and olaparib developed mismatch repair gene mutations leading to somatic hypermutation that included newly acquired EGFR, TP53, and other oncogenic mutations likely driving disease resistance and progression. Lastly, one other patient whose regimen included the MEK inhibitor trametinib developed newly acquired PIK3CA and PTEN mutations associated with a robust increase in phospho-S6 protein abundance corresponding to a RAS-MAPK pathway to PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway activation shift. Together, these findings indicate that diverse genetic mechanisms underlie therapeutic resistance to multiagent targeted therapy in GBM. However, in other patients, there was no identifiable genetic alteration or evolution after the trial regimen, thereby indicating that transcriptional and/or epigenetic evolution may also contribute to therapeutic resistance in GBM.

Several factors may contribute to the lack of significant survival benefit observed with our and other recent precision medicine clinical trials for GBM. Drug delivery across the blood-brain barrier and into tumor cells remains a major challenge in glioma treatment (39). Treatment resistance due to the genetic complexity of GBM and its ability to genetically evolve in response to targeted therapy likely limits the success of most single-agent targeted therapies. However, the toxicity from multidrug combinations can necessitate dose reduction or discontinuation of one or multiple agents, limiting drug exposure. Additionally, variability in assay methodologies may lead to inconsistent definitions of actionable molecular alterations, affecting patient selection and therapeutic responses. Drug selection differences between studies for the identical genetic alteration (e.g., using the CDK4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib versus ribociclib in the context of CDK4 amplification) or the differential prioritization of targeting one genetic alteration versus another (e.g., choosing to prioritize targeting the PIK3CA mutation over CDK4 amplification or vice versa) may also potentially contribute to differences in outcomes. Lastly, patient selection criteria and trial design differences, such as the inclusion of heterogeneous patient populations and variations in prior treatments, may contribute to discrepancies in survival benefits. Thus, the obstacles to treatment efficacy in patients with GBM are multifactorial in nature.

Nevertheless, recent studies highlight promising directions for GBM treatment, including adaptive platform trials and combination therapies (40, 41). For example, GBM AGILE is a global, multiarm, adaptive platform trial that employs a Bayesian adaptive design to evaluate multiple therapies in different arms, demonstrating feasibility, safety, and OS benefits with the inclusion of both patients with newly diagnosed GBM and rGBM (40). As our study has provided key foundational insight, these types of adaptive platform trials may help accelerate effective treatment discovery and enhance the efficacy of precision medicine due to their flexibility and ability to evaluate multiple therapies simultaneously. Additionally, comprehensive molecular profiling and a consensus on assay methodology for biomarker identification are needed to identify consistent targetable pathways for patients (2). Advancements in multiomic profiling, including single-cell transcriptomic and digital spatial profiling methodologies, may further refine patient stratification, ensuring therapies are directed toward molecular subgroups most likely to benefit (8, 42–44). A multiomic approach could provide a more comprehensive molecular profile and guidance in the development of an individualized regimen and assist in bridging the gap between molecular profiling and enhanced clinical results. Overcoming challenges like biomarker validation, tumor heterogeneity, and the blood-brain barrier remains critical to improving GBM outcomes.

This clinical trial and its underlying approach have limitations that must be acknowledged. First, though the number of formal DLTs was low, multiple patients experienced toxicities requiring dose reduction, discontinuation, or lack of initiation of one or multiple drugs in their regimen. This, in turn, not only limited exposure of the tumor to the selected drugs but also affected quality of life. Second, the cost of the medications may prohibit accessibility for many patients outside of a clinical trial setting. Although the cost of the drugs was covered as part of this clinical trial, next-stage testing of this type of approach in a larger clinical trial will be cost-prohibitive unless pharmaceutical companies are willing to provide drugs for use in testing individualized combination regimens. Moreover, if this approach is confirmed to be efficacious, efforts to obtain insurance authorization for an individualized combination are likely to be both difficult and time-consuming.

In summary, our precision medicine clinical trial for surgically resectable rGBM demonstrated feasibility and safety and met its primary efficacy endpoint of increased OS-9 compared with historical controls but did not clearly show a significant OS benefit versus traditional cytotoxic therapies in a contemporary patient cohort treated at our institution. These findings underscore the ongoing challenges in translating targeted, personalized treatments into meaningful survival improvements. Nonetheless, our study offers a fundamental framework for planning future personalized clinical trials in rGBM and, through longitudinal genomic profiling, identifies potential oncogenic resistance mechanisms to such targeted therapy regimens.
